payload.final_answer:
When you open a website in your browser, your computer needs to find the right computer on the internet to connect to. Every website lives on a computer with a special address called an IP address (like 192.168.1.1). However, you don't type numbers—you type a domain name like google.com.

DNS (Domain Name System) is the service that translates these website names into IP addresses. When you enter a website address, your computer asks a DNS server "What's the IP address for this website?" The DNS server looks it up and replies with the correct IP address, allowing your browser to connect to the right computer and load the website.

Analogy: DNS is like a phone directory—instead of remembering everyone's phone number, you look up their name and get their number.

Example: You type amazon.com into your browser. DNS translates "amazon.com" to IP address 205.251.242.103, and your browser connects to that address to load the website.
